newsitem.title: USA: U.S. income up but consumers hold off on spending.
newsitem.headline: U.S. income up but consumers hold off on spending.

text.p: U.S. income growth continued at a healthy pace in September but consumers remain hesitant to spend their new found wealth, opting instead to save, U.S. experts said.
"Income growth continues to be very solid but the spending that normally goes along with it has been relatively restrained," said Waldo Best, senior economist at BZW Securities Inc.
Earlier, the U.S. Commerce Department reported a 0.6 percent gain in September personal income and a modest 0.1 percent rise in consumption.
In a Reuter poll, U.S. economists had predicted a 0.6 percent gain in personal income and a 0.3 percent rise in consumption for last month.
"People are looking at this as a deferred consumption story," Best said. "Consumers are building up some type of savings or nest egg that at some point in time will turn into consumption."
Economists expect that the current buildup in savings will lead to some spending down the road in the form of big ticket item purchases, such as housing or durable goods.
However, others said consumption will take the form of soft goods such as traditional Christmas holiday purchases.

"Consumption down the road will probably take the form of soft goods purchases such as those affiliated with holiday spending," said Michelle Colley Lauglin, Treasury market specialist at Prudential Securities Inc.

"Consumers pulled back in the third quarter," Laughlin said. "With the savings rate at its highest level since December of '93 it looks as if the seed for the rebound in spending for the fourth quarter will have been sewn."
Meanwhile, economists noted that Wednesday's release of third quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by the Commerce Department had already shed some light on Thursday's consumption figure.
Commerce in its first estimate of third quarter GDP reported consumer spending up 0.4 percent, sharply lower then the second quarter's final reading of 3.4 percent.
Looking ahead, U.S. experts are predicting healthy Christmas sales as consumers continue to build up their nest eggs.
